Skip to content

Welcome

  • Features
  • Examples
  • Resources

This is a well-structured, accessible HTML5 document demonstrating modern best practices for semantic markup and inclusive design.

It uses semantic landmarks, a skip link for keyboard navigation, and CSS that adapts to your light or dark mode preference.

Text and link colors meet WCAG AA contrast in both themes, type scales with your browser's font size, and motion respects your system settings.

Features

  • Semantic HTML structure with proper landmarks
  • Keyboard accessible navigation and focus management
  • Dark mode support with custom color schemes
  • Responsive typography using modern CSS
  • Print-friendly styles for better readability
  • WCAG AA contrast compliance in all color modes

Examples

Component Cards

Card components are useful for organizing related content. They include a subtle border and padding for visual separation.

Learn more about accessibility resources

Interactive Elements

Buttons and links are fully accessible with clear focus states. All interactive elements include visible focus indicators and proper ARIA labels.

Keyboard navigation: Use Tab to move forward, Shift+Tab to move backward, and Enter to activate.

Accessible Form

Fields marked * are required.

For example, name@example.com
Up to 2,000 characters.

Live Region Example

Click the button to announce a message using a live region. This demonstrates how screen readers are notified of dynamic updates.

Interactive Counter

This counter demonstrates state management and ARIA live regions for accessible dynamic content.

0

  • HTML Living Standard (opens in new tab)
  • A11y 101 (opens in new tab)

lines: <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" spellcheck="false" autocapitalize="none" required aria-describedby="email-help">

content.text:
The page was already in good shape, so I made one change and found one issue that you should decide on.

**What I changed:** I removed `role="alert"` from the email error message (`0.html:496`). When someone submitted the form with a bad email, screen readers read the error twice: once from the alert, and again when the field got focus and read its linked error text. It also meant the error was read out as soon as the field lost focus, while the user was still moving through the form. Now the error is read once, when focus returns to the field after submit. This is the pattern GOV.UK uses. I haven't tested it with a screen reader.

**Needs your decision:** your email address (ksmith@centricle.com) is visible in the page source in two places: `<meta name="author">` (line 8) and the structured data block (line 25). Anyone can read it there, including spam bots. I'd suggest putting your name there instead, but I didn't change it because it's your call. Tell me what name to use and I'll update both.

I didn't find anything else worth changing. The contrast, dark mode, forced-colors, reduced-motion, print styles, focus handling and form hints are already well done, and more edits would just be churn.
